rationale: The student adds both numerators and denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). Showing hops on a number line marked in unit fractions of fifths clearly illustrates that adding fifths means moving along fifths, keeping the denominator constant at 5 while counting up the total number of parts.

script.focus: The tick marks stay fifths the entire time, so 1 fifth plus 3 fifths lands on 4 fifths, not tenths.

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: The tick marks stay fifths the entire time, so 1 fifth plus 3 fifths lands on 4 fifths, not tenths.

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The student added both numerators and denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). The demo clearly targets why the denominator remains fifths by visualizing addition as hops along a fixed number line of fifths, explicitly reinforcing that the size of the pieces does not change. Switching from an area/bar model to a number line provides a distinct, helpful representation.
judgement.verdict: Yes, a teacher would definitely use this visual number-line demo to show that adding fractional parts does not change their unit size.
